Empirical Research Plan – Effects of the 1989 Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement on Canadian Manufacturing  

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
-------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension (dynamic DID).

Why it fits  
• The policy arrived at a well-defined date (January 1 1989).  
• Industries differed widely in how much their bilateral tariff to the U.S. fell.  
• Annual panel data (industry × year) allow us to compare pre- vs. post-changes within an industry and across industries with high vs. low tariff cuts.  
• An event study will reveal short-, medium-, and long-run dynamics and let us test the parallel-trends assumption visually.

Continuous vs. binary treatment  
I will treat the size of the tariff reduction (ΔTariff_i) as a continuous “dose” of treatment. Estimates are thus semi-elasticities: β is the change in the outcome per one-percentage-point larger tariff cut. For transparency I will also show binary results (above-median cut = treated) as a robustness check.

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
-------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated_i = ΔTariff_i = (Most-Favoured Nation tariff in 1988 – negotiated CUSFTA tariff schedule in 1989) / 100.  
The larger the fall, the more an industry is exposed.

Control group / counterfactual  
Industries with zero or very small tariff cuts provide the counterfactual trend for high-cut industries. All regressions include industry and year fixed effects so that identification comes from differential changes.

Timing  
Post_t = 1 for 1989 and all subsequent years, 0 for 1980-1988. (We will additionally model leads and lags for event study: t = –5,…,+10.)

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
-------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of CUSFTA, high-cut and low-cut industries would have followed the same evolution in employment and productivity.  
Plausibility: Pre-1989 tariffs had been stable for years and no other Canada-specific policy was implemented exactly in 1989 that differentially targets high-tariff industries.

A2. No anticipatory effects: Firms did not adjust outcomes before 1989 in proportion to the upcoming tariff cut.  
Plausibility: The agreement was signed late 1988; implementation was 1 Jan 1989. This leaves little time for material re-allocation in 1988, but the event study will check for pre-trends.

A3. Stable unit composition: Industry classification and measurement of employment/output are consistent over time.  
Plausibility: Statistics Canada uses continuous SIC codes over our window; mergers re-coding is rare at 2-digit level. We will test robustness at both 3- and 4-digit levels.

A4. No treatment spillovers between industries: A tariff cut in industry i does not mechanically change measured employment/productivity in industry j except via general equilibrium effects that would be captured by year fixed effects.  
Plausibility: Some input–output linkages exist; we add input-output weighted tariff reductions of supplier industries as controls.

-------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Fixes  
-------------------------------------------------
T1 – Differential macro shocks (e.g., U.S. demand boom for certain goods).  
Fix: Include U.S. import-demand growth by industry as a control; also include world commodity-price controls.

T2 – Measurement error in tariff reductions (negotiated phase-out vs. actual).  
Fix: Use scheduled tariff cut in 1989 and also cumulative 5-year cut; instrument current tariffs with negotiated schedule to mitigate endogeneity of realized rates.

T3 – Industry reclassification / compositional change.  
Fix: Aggregate to stable 2-digit SIC; verify robustness at 3-digit; drop sectors that change codes.

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
-------------------------------------------------
```r
#---------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
#---------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # panel regressions
library(did)          # event-study tools
library(ggplot2)

#---------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
#---------------------------------------------
d <- fread("can_mfg_industry_1980_2000.csv")  # one row = industry-year
t <- fread("cusfta_tariff_cuts.csv")          # industry-level tariff schedules

#---------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
#---------------------------------------------
# merge
setkey(d, industry)
setkey(t, industry)
d <- t[d]

# Create outcome variables
d[, ln_emp := log(employment)]
d[, ln_prod := log(productivity)]

# Treatment intensity: percentage-point tariff cut from 1988 to 1989
d[, treat_intensity := tariff_1988 - tariff_1989]   # e.g. 4.5pp

# Post dummy and event-time dummies
d[, post := as.integer(year >= 1989)]
d[, rel_year := year - 1989]           # event time
for(L in -5:10){
  d[, paste0("leadlag_",L) := as.integer(rel_year==L)]
}

# Above-median binary treatment for robustness
cutoff <- median(d[year==1988, treat_intensity])
d[, treat_bin := as.integer(treat_intensity >= cutoff)]

#---------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID specification (continuous)
# Y_it = α_i + λ_t + β (ΔTariff_i × Post_t) + ε_it
#---------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(ln_emp ~ i(treat_intensity, post) | industry + year, 
                  data = d, cluster = "industry")
summary(did_main)

#---------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study (leads & lags)
#---------------------------------------------
# Interact treatment intensity with each lead/lag (omit -1 as baseline)
leadlag_vec <- paste0("i(rel_year, treat_intensity, ref = -1)")
event_mod <- feols(ln_emp ~ fe(reg = industry) + fe(year) | industry + year, data = d)
# Alternatively use 'did' package for automatic
es <- att_gt(yname = "ln_emp",
             tname = "year",
             idname = "industry",
             gname = "g",          # first year treated - use tariff bin groups
             xformla = ~0,
             data = d)
# plot pre/post
# ...

#---------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: binary treatment & placebo years
#---------------------------------------------
did_binary <- feols(ln_emp ~ treat_bin*post | industry + year, data = d, cluster = "industry")
placebo <- feols(ln_emp ~ i(treat_intensity, year==1986) | industry + year, 
                 data = d[year<=1988], cluster = "industry")

#---------------------------------------------
# 6. Output table
#---------------------------------------------
etable(list(did_main, did_binary, placebo),
       dict = c("treat_intensity:post"="TariffCut×Post",
                "treat_bin:post"="HighCut×Post"),
       tex = FALSE)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
-------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts trade liberalisation reallocates resources toward more productive industries and raises overall TFP while reducing employment in low-productivity, high-tariff sectors. Therefore:  
• Employment: β < 0. A one-percentage-point larger tariff cut may lower industry employment by roughly 0.3–0.6 percent in the short run; effect may attenuate in the long run as surviving firms expand.  
• Productivity (TFP or labour productivity): β > 0. Expect +0.2–0.4 percent per 1 pp larger tariff cut within five years, potentially larger long-run gains if selection pushes up average productivity.

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Difference-in-Differences)  
C1  Parallel pre-trends visually verified ................... 1  
C2  No anticipation (no significant leads) .................. 0.8  
C3  Stable composition of units (industries) ................ 0.8  
C4  No time-varying confounders correlated with treatment ... 0.6  
C5  Correct inference (clustered SE at industry level) ...... 1  
Overall ≈ 4.2 / 5  

I would therefore regard the empirical design as high quality but remain vigilant about residual confounding macro shocks (C4).
